title_en: Zhao Donghong, Zhang Ruyi, and Third Party Zou Jihao v. Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office — administrative dispute over patent invalidation
ruling_gist_en: Article 22 of the Patent Law of the PRC provides: "An invention or utility model for which a patent right is granted shall possess novelty, inventiveness, and practical applicability." For invention or utility model patents, it is necessary to establish reasonable standards for determining inventiveness. The inventiveness standards for invention patents and utility model patents are different, so the scope of prior art considered in technical comparison should also differ. Considering that the inventiveness standard for utility model patents is relatively low, the scope of prior art considered when evaluating inventiveness should be narrower, and generally, the prior art in the technical field to which the utility model patent belongs should be primarily compared. However, where the prior art already provides a clear technical teaching prompting a person of ordinary skill in the art to seek relevant technical means from a similar or related technical field, prior art in such similar or related technical fields may also be considered.

full_text_en:
Zhao Donghong, Zhang Ruyi, and Third Party Zou Jihao v.  
Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office  

— Administrative Dispute over Patent Invalidation  

【Ruling Summary】  

Article 22 of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "Inventions and utility models for which patent rights are granted shall possess novelty, inventiveness and practical applicability." For inventions or utility model patents, a reasonable standard for assessing inventiveness must be established. The inventiveness standards for invention patents and utility model patents are different; accordingly, the scope of prior art to be considered in technical comparison should also differ. Given the lower inventiveness standard for utility model patents, the scope of prior art to be considered in assessing their inventiveness should be narrower. Generally, comparison should primarily focus on prior art in the technical field to which the utility model patent pertains. However, where prior art has provided a clear technical teaching that would prompt a person of ordinary skill in the art to seek relevant technical means in a related or similar technical field, prior art in such related or similar technical fields may also be considered.  

Administrative Ruling of the Supreme People's Court  

(2011) Xing Zi Zi No. 19  

Applicant for Retrial (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office. Address: Yin'ge Building, No. 9, West Road of North Fourth Ring, Haidian District, Beijing.  

Legal Representative: Zhang Maoyu, Deputy Director of the Board.  

Agent ad litem: Liu Yabin, Examiner of the Board.  

Agent ad litem: Wang Jing, Examiner of the Board.  

Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Zhao Donghong, male, Han ethnicity, born June 15, 1962, residing at Room 22, Building 1, Door 1, No. 2, West Street of Fengtai Town, Fengtai District, Beijing, General Manager of Beijing Xindong Huateng Sports Equipment Co., Ltd.  

Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Zhang Ruyi, male, Han ethnicity, born November 11, 1934, residing at Room 404, Apartment 17, Tsinghua University, Haidian District, Beijing, retired teacher of Tsinghua University.  

Third Party at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance: Zou Jihao, male, Han ethnicity, born June 5, 1940, residing at Room 3-3-1, No. 182, Lingshui Road, Ganjingzi District, Dalian City, Liaoning Province, retired teacher of the Institute of Physical Education, Dalian University of Technology.  

The applicant for retrial, the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Reexamination Board), dissented from the administrative judgment (2010) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 811 rendered by the Beijing Higher People's Court (hereinafter referred to as the court of second instance) in the case of administrative dispute over patent invalidation with respondents Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi and the third party at first instance, appellee at second instance, Zou Jihao, and filed an application for retrial with this Court. This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel to examine the case, which has now been concluded.  

On November 6, 2008, the Patent Reexamination Board made Decision No. 12613 on the Review of the Request for Invalidation Declaration (hereinafter referred to as the Decision under Review), finding that the utility model patent titled "Grip Strength Meter" (Patent No. 97216613.0) did not comply with the provisions of Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Law), and declared the patent in question wholly invalid. Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi, dissatisfied with the Decision under Review, filed an administrative lawsuit with the Beijing First Intermediate People's Court (hereinafter referred to as the court of first instance).  

After trial, the court of first instance held that the facts found in the Decision under Review were clear, the law was correctly applied, and the review procedure was lawful, and thus the decision should be upheld; the claims of Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi were not established, and their request to revoke the Decision under Review was not supported. Accordingly, in accordance with Article 54(1) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court ruled to uphold the Decision under Review.  

Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, appealed to the Beijing Higher People's Court (hereinafter referred to as the court of second instance), arguing: First, the Patent Reexamination Board, without a request from Zou Jihao, investigated and collected evidence on its own and deprived the appellants of their right to respond to the evidence collected, thereby violating the principle of administrative hearing. Second, the Decision under Review, in determining that the Chinese utility model patent with an authorization publication date of September 4, 1996 and authorization publication number CN2234609Y (i.e., Evidence 2 in the Decision under Review) belonged to the same technical field as the patent in question, used this as a basis for finding a lack of inventiveness in the patent in question, which lacked factual basis. Therefore, the Decision under Review had unclear findings of fact and the administrative procedure was unlawful; the judgment of first instance upholding it was erroneous. They requested that the court of second instance revoke the judgment of first instance and the Decision under Review.  

The Patent Reexamination Board argued that the Decision under Review was correct and the procedure lawful; the judgment of first instance upholding the Decision under Review had clear facts and correctly applied the law. It requested that the court of second instance dismiss the appeal and uphold the judgment of first instance.  

Zou Jihao submitted that the facts in the Decision under Review were clear and that the judgment of first instance upholding it was correct. He requested that the court of second instance dismiss the appeal and uphold the judgment of first instance.  

The court of second instance confirmed the following facts:  

On May 28, 1997, Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi filed a utility model patent application with the State Intellectual Property Office for a "Grip Strength Meter." On September 23, 1998, the State Intellectual Property Office granted them the patent right, i.e., the patent in question. The claims as published in the patent authorization announcement for the patent in question are as follows:  

1. A grip strength meter, comprising: an outer grip handle, an inner grip handle installed within the outer grip handle, a force measuring sensor connected to the inner grip handle, and a detection and display device installed within a housing, characterized in that the force measuring sensor is an elastic beam with a plurality of bosses, and the force measuring sensor is connected to the inner grip handle via a grip distance adjustment device.  

2. The grip strength meter according to claim 1, characterized in that the elastic beam has three bosses, and the bosses at the two ends protrude higher than the middle boss.  

3. The grip strength meter according to claim 1 or 2, characterized in that a force bearing plate is provided on the boss side of the elastic beam.  

4. The grip strength meter according to claim 3, characterized in that the elastic beam and the force bearing plate form an integral frame structure.  

5. The grip strength meter according to any one of claims 1, 2, or 4, characterized in that the grip distance adjustment device is a force rod with a distance adjustment handwheel, the force rod passing through the outer grip handle to connect the inner grip handle and the force measuring sensor.  

6. The grip strength meter according to claim 3, characterized in that positioning bosses are provided on the outer sides of the two side frames of the inner grip handle, and the positioning bosses are installed in sliding grooves of the outer grip handle.  

On April 28, 2008, Zou Jihao filed a request for a declaration of invalidation with the Patent Reexamination Board, on the grounds that the patent in question did not comply with Article 22, Paragraph 3, Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law, and Article 20, Paragraph 1, Article 21, Paragraph 2 of the Detailed Rules for the Implementation of the Patent Law, and submitted six pieces of evidence:  

Evidence 1: Japanese Unexamined Utility Model Publication No. Hei 4-131217, published on December 2, 1992;  
Evidence 2: Chinese Utility Model Patent Specification No. CN2234609Y, published on September 4, 1996;  
Evidence 3: Chinese Invention Patent Application Publication No. CN1076779A, published on September 29, 1993;  
Evidence 4: Copies (5 pages) of the copyright page and pages 247, 260, 275, 279 of the "Sensor Technology Handbook," edited by Yuan Xiguang, published by National Defense Industry Press, first edition December 1986, second printing January 1989;  
Evidence 5: The authorized publication text of the patent in question;  
Evidence 6: Japanese Patent Publication No. Hei 4-10816, published on February 26, 1992.  

After accepting the request, the Patent Reexamination Board forwarded the relevant documents to Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi and requested that they submit their opinions on the invalidation request within one month. Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi did not respond within the specified period.  

On May 27, 2008, Zou Jihao submitted a statement of opinion, along with supplementary submissions including Chinese translations of Evidence 1 and 6, Japanese Unexamined Patent Publication No. Sho 60-207640 and its Chinese translation (hereinafter Evidence 7), and Japanese Unexamined Utility Model Publication No. Sho 60-153104, published on October 12, 1985, and its Chinese translation (hereinafter Evidence 8).  

The Patent Reexamination Board forwarded the above documents submitted by Zou Jihao. On August 5, 2008, Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi submitted a statement of opinion.  

On September 16, 2008, Zou Jihao submitted another statement of opinion, along with copies of pages 200-201 of Evidence 4 and copies (3 pages) of the copyright page and pages 73, 83 of the book "Sensor Engineering," edited by Wang Hongye and published by National University of Defense Technology Press, first edition, first printing April 1997 (hereinafter Evidence 9), Chinese Utility Model Patent Specification No. CN87212699U, published on August 10, 1988 (hereinafter Evidence 10), and Chinese Utility Model Patent Application Specification No. CN2045270U, published on October 4, 1989 (hereinafter Evidence 11).  

On September 25, 2008, the Patent Reexamination Board conducted an oral hearing. Both Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi, and Zou Jihao authorized agents to participate in the hearing. During the oral hearing, Zou Jihao clearly stated that they waived the use of Evidence 8 and indicated that Evidence 9-11 and the supplementary pages 200-201 of Evidence 4 were used to prove common general knowledge. At the same time, Zou Jihao clearly defined the combinations of evidence for evaluating the inventiveness of the patent in question, i.e., using Evidence 6 in combination with Evidence 2, Evidence 1 in combination with Evidence 2, Evidence 1 in combination with common general knowledge, and Evidence 2 in combination with Evidence 7 to assess the inventiveness of claim 1 of the patent in question; Evidence 4, Evidence 9, and Evidence 2 disclosed the additional features of dependent claims 2-4; Evidence 1 and Evidence 6 disclosed the additional features of dependent claims 5 and 6; Evidence 7 also disclosed the additional features of dependent claim 5; the additional features of dependent claim 6 also belonged to common general knowledge; and Evidence 3 was used to prove that bosses were common general knowledge. The Patent Reexamination Board informed both parties that since Evidence 10 and 11 submitted by Zou Jihao exceeded the time limit for submitting evidence and did not constitute evidence of common general knowledge, they would not be considered. Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi had no objection to the authenticity of Evidence 2-5 and 9, but raised objections to the authenticity and accuracy of the translations of Evidence 1, 6, and 7. The Patent Reexamination Board informed Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi that they could submit written statements regarding the authenticity and translation accuracy of Evidence 1, 6, and 7 within 15 days after the conclusion of the oral hearing; failure to submit within the time limit would be deemed as no objection.  

After the oral hearing, on October 7, 2008, Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi submitted a statement of opinion, arguing that the Japanese patent documents submitted by Zou Jihao could not be found in the database of the Japan Patent Office website. Moreover, the Japanese patent documents submitted by Zou Jihao were evidence formed in Japan, but Zou Jihao did not submit notarized and authenticated certification procedures, nor did he submit patent documents obtained from the patent office. Therefore, they requested that the evidence not be considered.  

Regarding the evidence submitted by Zou Jihao, the Patent Reexamination Board, after examination, found that Evidence 2 was a Chinese utility model patent specification published before the filing date of the patent in question, and Evidence 5 was the authorized publication text of the patent in question. Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi had no objection to the authenticity of Evidence 2 and 5. Upon examination, the Patent Reexamination Board found that Evidence 2 and 5 were authentic and credible and could be used as evidence in this case. The content recorded in Evidence 2 constituted prior art for the patent in question, and Evidence 5 served as the basis for the invalidation request review. Evidence 7 was a Japanese unexamined patent publication, and Zou Jihao submitted a Chinese translation of that evidence. Evidence 7 was a Japanese patent document published before the filing date of the patent in question. Any person in China could obtain the document by querying the official website of the Japan Patent Office via the internet. Therefore, the Patent Reexamination Board found that Evidence 7 fell under the circumstance (1) of Section 2.2.2, Chapter 8, Part IV of the "Guidelines for Examination," and did not require related certification procedures. The Patent Reexamination Board verified that the full text of Evidence 7 could be found on the official website of the Japan Patent Office and was consistent with the text submitted by Zou Jihao, thus recognizing the authenticity of Evidence 7. Regarding the objection raised by Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi that the handwriting in Evidence 7 was blurred and difficult to read, the Patent Reexamination Board found that the handwriting in Evidence 7 submitted by Zou Jihao was clear and legible and there was no difficulty in reading; moreover, Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi did not specifically point out which parts of Evidence 7 were difficult to read. Since Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi did not raise specific objections to the Chinese translation of Evidence 7 within the specified period, they were deemed to have no objection to the accuracy of the Chinese translation of Evidence 7. Therefore, the Patent Reexamination Board found that Evidence 7 could be used as evidence in this case, the content recorded therein constituted prior art for the patent in question, and the textual content shall be based on the Chinese translation submitted by Zou Jihao.  

Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law provides: "Inventiveness means that, compared with the technology existing before the filing date, the invention has prominent substantive features and represents notable progress, and the utility model has substantive features and represents progress."  

If a technical solution of a claim has distinguishing technical features compared with the prior art disclosed in one piece of evidence, and those distinguishing technical features are disclosed by prior art in another piece of evidence belonging to the same technical field, and the feature plays the same role in that other evidence as it does in the patent, then the claim lacks inventiveness.  

Specifically in this case, claim 1 of the patent in question seeks to protect a grip strength meter. The technical problem to be solved is to provide a grip strength meter that is accurate in detection, simple in structure, and easy to operate. The technical solution of claim 1 is: a grip strength meter, comprising: an outer grip handle, an inner grip handle installed within the outer grip handle, a force measuring sensor connected to the inner grip handle, and a detection and display device installed within a housing, characterized in that the force measuring sensor is an elastic beam with a plurality of bosses, and the force measuring sensor is connected to the inner grip handle via a grip distance adjustment device.  

Evidence 7 discloses a physical strength tester, specifically disclosing the following: the physical strength tester includes: an outer grip portion (corresponding to the outer grip handle of the patent in question), a middle grip portion installed within the outer grip portion (corresponding to the inner grip handle of the patent in question), one end of a compression screw (corresponding to the grip distance adjustment device of the patent in question) is connected to the middle grip portion via an adjustment handwheel and is freely rotatable, and the other end is screwed into a cylindrical body provided at the base end of a compression plate of a compression spring, the compression plate and a rack are integrally connected via a rack rod, the rack meshes with a pinion fixed on a rotating shaft of a rotary encoder (the compression spring, compression plate, cylindrical body, rack rod, rack, rotary encoder, and pinion as a whole correspond to the force measuring sensor of the patent in question); during measurement, the subject grips the middle grip portion and the outer grip portion, the spring is compressed via the compression plate and descends, while the rack rod integrated with the compression plate moves, the rack meshed therewith also descends, the pinion meshing with the rack rotates on the rotating shaft of the rotary encoder, the rotation angle increases in proportion to the grip strength, thereby generating square wave pulses proportional to the angle in the rotary encoder, which are transmitted to a device (corresponding to the detection and display device of the patent in question) that digitally displays the muscle strength measurement, thus completing the grip strength measurement.  

From the above, it can be seen that compared with the content disclosed in Evidence 7, the technical solution of claim 1 of the patent in question has the following differences: (1) The force measuring sensor in claim 1 of the patent in question is an elastic beam with a plurality of bosses, while in Evidence 7, a structure consisting of a compression spring, compression plate, rack rod, rack, rotary encoder, and pinion is used to realize the function of the force measuring sensor; (2) The detection and display device in claim 1 of the patent in question is installed within a housing, while Evidence 7 does not explicitly record the installation position of the display device.  

Evidence 2 discloses a portable digital display electronic scale, specifically disclosing that the electronic scale includes a weighing hook, hanging ring, housing, and weighing sensor. The weighing sensor is an M-type sensor processed from a metal elastic body with its center of gravity in the middle. From Figure 4, it can be seen that the M-type sensor has three leg-like structures extending vertically downward (corresponding to the plurality of bosses of the force measuring sensor of the patent in question), wherein the leg-like structures on both sides are integrally formed with a bottom plate, the middle leg-like structure is shorter and does not contact the bottom plate, four resistance strain gauges are attached to the surface of the M-type sensor, and the housing is provided with a display screen, which is driven by multiple electrical components within the housing to display the weight of the object being weighed.  

It can be seen that Evidence 2 already discloses an M-type sensor with three leg-like structures extending vertically downward, and since the M-type sensor is processed from a metal elastic body, it must be elastic. Therefore, this is equivalent to disclosing that the force measuring sensor of the patent in question is an elastic beam with a plurality of bosses; and the display screen and the circuit elements driving the display screen in Evidence 2 are equivalent to disclosing the detection and display device installed within the housing of the patent in question. Thus, the above distinguishing technical features (1) and (2) are both disclosed by Evidence 2. Moreover, Evidence 2, the patent in question, and Evidence 7 all belong to the technical field of force measuring devices. The difference between measuring gravity in Evidence 2 and measuring grip strength in the patent in question and Evidence 7 lies only in that gravity is applied by the object being weighed, while grip strength is applied by the subject's hand. However, the direction of the applied gravity and grip strength is both vertically downward. That is to say, the gravity in Evidence 2 and the grip strength in the patent in question and Evidence 7 differ only in the object applying the force, and the difference in the object applying the force does not materially affect the measurement of the gravity or grip strength; in other words, the measurement principles of the gravity and grip strength are substantially the same. Furthermore, in the actual design of force measuring devices, both gravity measuring devices and grip strength measuring devices are realized by using commonly used pressure sensors or tension sensors in the field of force measurement. For a person skilled in the art, replacing the sensor structure in the grip strength measuring device with the pressure sensor in the gravity measuring device does not require inventive effort. Therefore, on the basis of Evidence 7, a person skilled in the art would readily think of replacing the multiple components used to realize the sensor function in Evidence 7 with the M-type sensor in Evidence 2 and installing the display device within the housing, thereby obtaining the technical solution of claim 1 of the patent in question. That is, combining Evidence 7 with Evidence 2 to obtain the technical solution of claim 1 of the patent in question is obvious to a person skilled in the art. Therefore, claim 1 of the patent in question lacks inventiveness relative to the combination of Evidence 7 and Evidence 2 and does not comply with Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law.  

Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi argued that Evidence 2 and the patent in question are not in the same technical field, it is used for weighing, and there is no teaching for combination; Figure 4 of Evidence 2 only shows one boss; Evidence 7 does not describe grip distance. Therefore, claim 1 of the patent in question possesses inventiveness.

In this regard, the Patent Reexamination Board held that, as previously stated, Evidence 2, the patent in dispute, and Evidence 7 all belong to the technical field of force measuring devices. The gravity in Evidence 2 and the grip strength in the patent in dispute and Evidence 7 differ only in the object to which force is applied, and this difference does not substantially affect the measurement of such gravity and grip strength, meaning that the measurement principles for gravity and grip strength are not substantially different. Therefore, a person of ordinary skill in the art would be motivated to combine Evidence 2 with Evidence 7. The three leg-like structures extending vertically downward from the M-type sensor in Evidence 2 correspond to the multiple protrusions described in the patent in dispute. Although Evidence 7 does not explicitly state that the compression screw is used to adjust the grip distance, it can be determined from the description of the compression screw and the adjustment handwheel in the specification of Evidence 7, together with Figure 1, that turning the adjustment handwheel causes the compression screw to rotate, thereby driving the inner grip to move up or down, thus adjusting the grip distance between the inner grip and the outer grip. Therefore, the compression screw in Evidence 7 corresponds to the disclosure of the grip distance adjustment device of the patent in dispute. In summary, the arguments of Zhao Donghong and Zhang Ruyi cannot stand.

Claim 2 is a dependent claim referring to Claim 1, with the additional technical feature that "the elastic beam has three protrusions, and the protrusions at the two ends extend higher than the middle protrusion." It can be seen from Figure 4 of Evidence 2 that the leg-like structures on both sides of the M-type sensor are longer than the middle leg-like structure, thereby suspending the middle leg-like structure. Therefore, this feature has also been disclosed by Evidence 2, and it serves the same function in Evidence 2 as in Claim 2 of the present application. Since Claim 1 lacks inventiveness, its dependent Claim 2 also lacks inventiveness as provided in Article 22(3) of the Patent Law relative to the combination of Evidence 7 and Evidence 2.

Claim 3 is a dependent claim referring to Claim 1 or 2, with the additional technical feature that "a force-bearing plate is provided on the side of the protrusions of the elastic beam." It can be seen from Figure 4 of Evidence 2 that at the bottom of the leg-like structures of the M-type sensor, there is a bottom plate (corresponding to the force-bearing plate described in Claim 3) that connects with the leg-like structures on both sides of the M-type sensor. Therefore, this feature has also been disclosed by Evidence 2. Since Claim 1 or 2 lacks inventiveness, its dependent Claim 3 also lacks inventiveness as provided in Article 22(3) of the Patent Law relative to the combination of Evidence 7 and Evidence 2.

Claim 4 is a dependent claim referring to Claim 3, with the additional technical feature that "the elastic beam and the force-bearing plate form an integral frame structure." It can be seen from Figure 4 of Evidence 2 that the leg-like structures of the M-type sensor are formed integrally with the bottom plate. Therefore, this feature has also been disclosed by Evidence 2. Since Claim 3 lacks inventiveness, its dependent Claim 4 also lacks inventiveness as provided in Article 22(3) of the Patent Law relative to the combination of Evidence 7 and Evidence 2.

Claim 5 is a dependent claim referring to any one of Claims 1, 2, or 4, with the additional technical feature that "the grip distance adjustment device is a force rod with a distance adjustment handwheel, the force rod passes through the outer grip, and connects the inner grip with the force sensor." Evidence 7 discloses a compression screw (corresponding to the force rod described in Claim 5) and an adjustment handwheel (corresponding to the distance adjustment handwheel described in Claim 5) provided at the front end of the compression screw. The compression screw passes through the outer grip portion and connects the middle grip portion with the cylindrical body provided on the compression plate (from the previous analysis of Claim 1, it is known that the compression plate and the cylindrical body thereon are parts used to realize the sensor function in Evidence 7, thus corresponding to the disclosure of the connection relationship described in Claim 5). Therefore, the above additional technical features have also been disclosed by Evidence 7. Since Claim 1, 2, or 4 lacks inventiveness, its dependent Claim 5 also lacks inventiveness as provided in Article 22(3) of the Patent Law relative to the combination of Evidence 7 and Evidence 2.

Claim 6 is a dependent claim referring to Claim 3, with the additional technical feature that "positioning protrusions are provided on the outer sides of the side frames of the inner grip, and the positioning protrusions are installed in sliding slots of the outer grip." The function of the above additional technical features is to ensure that the inner grip can only move in the direction of the sliding slots through the engagement of the positioning protrusions and the sliding slots. In order to make the inner grip move toward the lower end of the outer grip in the same plane as the outer grip when force is applied, without tilting to avoid measurement errors, a person of ordinary skill in the art would be able to conceive of the measure of providing sliding slots on the outer grip and positioning protrusions on the side frames of the inner grip, thereby making the inner grip engage with the sliding slots of the outer grip without tilting movement. This is a common technical means in the art. Therefore, since Claim 3 lacks inventiveness, its dependent Claim 6 also lacks inventiveness as provided in Article 22(3) of the Patent Law relative to the combination of Evidence 7, Evidence 2, and common general knowledge.

In summary, Claims 1-6 of the patent in dispute lack inventiveness and do not comply with Article 22(3) of the Patent Law. Having reached the conclusion that all claims of the patent in dispute lack inventiveness, the Patent Reexamination Board did not further evaluate other evidence and arguments submitted by Zou Jihao.

Based on the above reasons, the Patent Reexamination Board made the Decision under Review on November 6, 2008, declaring the entire patent in dispute invalid.

Separately, on March 3, 2008, the Patent Reexamination Board, in response to the invalidity examination request from Shenzhen Haohao Family Industrial Co., Ltd., made Decision No. 11088, holding that the patent in dispute and the Chinese utility model patent specification with the authorization announcement date of September 4, 1996 and the authorization announcement number CN2234609Y (i.e., Evidence 2 in the Decision under Review) "belong to different technical fields, and there are differences in the invention purposes and the force application directions of the sensors between the two, and a person of ordinary skill in the art could not easily conceive of applying a sensor from another technical field to the present field."

The court of second instance held that the parties had no objection to the examination duties of the Patent Reexamination Board, and upon examination, confirmed them. Given that the evidence on which the Decision under Review was based was all examined during the oral hearing, the Patent Reexamination Board's examination and verification of the evidence based on the appellant's examination opinions did not violate the relevant provisions of the Patent Examination Guidelines. The court of second instance, upon examination, confirmed the legality of the procedure for making the Decision under Review. The focus of dispute in this case is whether the Decision under Review's determination that the patent in dispute and Evidence 2 belong to the same technical field and thereby negating the inventiveness of the patent in dispute is correct.

When assessing whether a utility model patent possesses inventiveness, consideration is generally focused on the technical field to which the utility model patent belongs. In this case, the patent in dispute claims a grip dynamometer, and the technical problem to be solved is to provide a grip dynamometer with accurate detection, simple structure, and convenient operation. Evidence 2 discloses a portable digital display electronic scale, which is a device for measuring gravity. There are differences in the invention purposes and the force application directions of the sensors between the two, and they belong to different technical fields. A person of ordinary skill in the art could not easily conceive of applying a sensor from another technical field to the present field. Moreover, Decision No. 11088 made by the Patent Reexamination Board has already clearly determined that the patent in dispute and Evidence 2 "belong to different technical fields." In the absence of the validity of Decision No. 11088 being negated through any legal procedure, the Patent Reexamination Board made a different judgment on the same situation, which runs counter to the principle of lawful administration requiring consistency and not being capricious. Therefore, the Decision under Review, which negated the inventiveness of the patent in dispute by combining Evidence 7 with Evidence 2, which is not in the same technical field as the patent in dispute, constituted an error in fact finding. The first instance judgment erred in determining that the patent in dispute and Evidence 2 belong to the same technical field and on that basis, upholding the Decision under Review.

The court of second instance, pursuant to Article 61(3) and Article 54(2)(1) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, ordered as follows: 1. The Administrative Judgment (2009) Yi Zhong Xing Chu Zi No. 466 of the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court is reversed; 2. Decision No. 12613 on Invalidity Declaration Request Examination made by the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office on November 6, 2008 is reversed; 3. The Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office shall make a new decision on the invalidity declaration request examination for this case. The court acceptance fees for the first and second instances, each RMB 100, shall be borne by the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office.

The Patent Reexamination Board applied for retrial, alleging that the second instance judgment had unclear findings of fact and erroneous application of law. Its main reasons: 1. Regarding the technical field. According to Part IV, Chapter 6, Section 4 of the Patent Examination Guidelines, for utility model patents, consideration is generally focused on the technical field to which the utility model patent belongs. However, if the prior art provides a clear suggestion, for example, explicit records in the prior art that prompt a person of ordinary skill in the art to look for relevant technical means in adjacent or relevant technical fields, the adjacent or relevant technical fields may be considered. The patent in dispute claims a grip dynamometer for measuring human grip strength. Evidence 2 discloses a portable digital display scale. The force application direction and the structure of the sensors in the two are the same. The only difference lies in the object to which force is applied during measurement. Broadly speaking, both belong to the technical field of force measuring devices. Considering the final product forms of the two, they should also belong to adjacent technical fields. In the actual design of force measuring devices, both gravity measuring devices and grip strength measuring devices commonly use pressure sensors or tension sensors commonly used in the field of force measurement. For a person of ordinary skill in the art, it would be easy to conceive of replacing the sensors, which is obvious and requires no inventive effort. 2. The Patent Reexamination Board's proactive correction of the erroneous determination in the prior decision complies with the principle and spirit of lawful administration.

This Court holds that the legislative purpose of the Patent Law is to protect the legitimate rights and interests of patentees, encourage inventions and creations, promote the application of inventions and creations, enhance innovation capabilities, and promote scientific and technological progress and economic and social development. It is evident that the patent system must not only protect the legitimate rights and interests of patentees but also fully consider the legitimate rights and interests of the public, thereby achieving a balance between the two. To achieve the aforementioned balance, reasonable patent grant standards need to be established. For inventions or utility models, reasonable inventiveness judgment standards need to be established. If the inventiveness standard is set too low, patent applications with low levels of innovation will more easily obtain grants or be difficult to be declared invalid, which will inevitably restrict the dissemination and utilization of technology, be detrimental to scientific and technological progress and social development, and harm the public interest. If the inventiveness standard is set too high, the difficulty of obtaining patent grants will greatly increase, which will diminish the incentive effect of patent law on technological innovation. Article 22 of the Patent Law provides that inventiveness of an invention means that, compared with the prior art, the invention has prominent substantive features and represents significant progress; inventiveness of a utility model means that the utility model has substantive features and progress. The inventiveness standard for utility model patents stipulated by the Patent Law is lower than that for invention patents. Whether an invention creation has inventiveness should be judged based on the knowledge and abilities of a person of ordinary skill in the art in the technical field to which it pertains, and by comparing the technical solution of the invention creation with the prior art. The inventiveness standards for invention patents and utility model patents differ, and therefore, the scope of prior art considered during technical comparison should also differ. This is an important aspect reflecting the difference in inventiveness standards between invention patents and utility model patents.

A technical field should be the specific technical field to which the technical solution of the claimed invention or utility model pertains or is applied, not a broader or adjacent technical field, nor the invention or utility model itself. The patent in dispute is a utility model patent titled "Grip Dynamometer." To judge whether it possesses inventiveness, the technical field to which the grip dynamometer belongs, as well as related and adjacent technical fields, should first be determined. The determination of the technical field should be based on the content defined by the claims, generally determined by the subject matter name of the patent, combined with the technical function and purpose realized by the technical solution. The lowest position of the patent in the International Patent Classification is of reference significance for determining its technical field. Adjacent technical fields generally refer to fields where the function and specific purpose of the utility model patent product are similar. Related technical fields generally refer to the functional fields where the distinguishing technical features between the utility model patent and the closest prior art are applied. The technical function of the patent in dispute belongs to force measuring devices, with the specific purpose of measuring human grip strength.

Since the division of the scope of technical fields is closely related to the level of inventiveness required, and considering that the inventiveness standard for utility model patents is relatively low, the scope of the prior art to be considered when evaluating its inventiveness should be narrower. Generally, the prior art in the technical field to which the utility model patent belongs should be primarily compared. However, under circumstances where the prior art has already provided a clear technical suggestion, prompting a person of ordinary skill in the art to look for relevant technical means in adjacent or relevant technical fields, prior art in adjacent or relevant technical fields may also be considered. The so-called clear technical suggestion refers to a technical suggestion explicitly recorded in the prior art or a technical suggestion that a person of ordinary skill in the art can determine directly and unequivocally from the prior art.

In this case, compared with the content disclosed in Evidence 7 (a physical strength measuring device), which is the closest prior art, the technical solution of Claim 1 of the patent in dispute has the distinguishing technical feature of a different force sensor; the force sensing device is in the related technical field of the patent in dispute. To evaluate the inventiveness of the force sensor, the Patent Reexamination Board considered Evidence 2 (a portable digital display electronic scale for measuring gravity) and compared its force sensor with the sensor of the patent in dispute. Although a grip dynamometer and an electronic scale are both force measuring devices, they have different specific purposes. At the same time, comparing gravity and human grip strength, the object to which force is applied differs, and the direction of force application also differs. Gravity is purely downward, while human grip strength is not purely downward but from all directions toward the center. Therefore, the two do not belong to the same technical field. However, the patent in dispute and the portable digital display electronic scale have the same function and similar purposes, and the force measurement principles of their force sensors are basically the same. The portable digital display electronic scale can be considered as an adjacent technical field of the patent in dispute. However, since the prior art did not provide a clear technical suggestion, the Patent Reexamination Board's consideration of the force sensor of the portable electronic scale in evaluating the inventiveness of the patent in dispute constituted an erroneous application of law.

In summary, the retrial application of the Patent Reexamination Board does not meet the conditions set forth in Article 63(2) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 72 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. Pursuant to Article 74 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, it is ordered as follows:

The retrial application of the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office is dismissed.
